TRUSTEE LIABILITY FOR BREACH OF TRUST — REMEDIES, MEASURE OF LIABILITY, AND EXCULPATORY CLAUSES (PROB. CODE §§ 16400-16465; UZYEL V. KADISHA; NOGGLE V. BANK OF AMERICA; PEOPLE EX REL. HARRIS V. SHINE) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for the Lindeman Family Trust · June 14, 2011

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes what California law provides about a trustee's liability to the beneficiaries of a trust for a breach of trust: what the Probate Code counts as a breach of trust; when a trustee is answerable for the acts of an agent, of a cotrustee, or of a predecessor trustee; what proceedings a beneficiary or cotrustee may bring when a breach is committed or threatened; how the Probate Code measures what a trustee who has committed a breach is chargeable with, including loss to the trust estate, profit the trustee made, and profit the trust would have made; when interest runs on such an award and at what rate; when a court may excuse a trustee from that liability; how long a beneficiary has to bring a claim after receiving an account or report; and the four ways the Probate Code allows a trustee's liability to be narrowed or discharged — an exculpatory provision in the trust instrument, a shortened period to object to an account, the written directions of a person holding the power to revoke, and a beneficiary's own consent, release, or affirmance — together with the limits the statutes place on each. It is prepared as background in connection with the Lindeman Family Trust dated June 14, 2011, the administration of that trust by Gregory T. Ahn, and any proceeding concerning it in Santa Clara County, California. It states what the statutes and the published opinions say. It does not state whether any particular act or omission was a breach of trust, what any trust instrument means, whether any claim is timely, or what any person should do.

WHAT COUNTS AS A BREACH OF TRUST (PROB. CODE § 16400)
Probate Code section 16400 states the whole of California's definition in one sentence: a violation by the trustee of any duty that the trustee owes the beneficiary is a breach of trust. The section does not list the duties; those are set out elsewhere in the Probate Code and in the trust instrument, and they include the duties to administer the trust according to its terms, to act loyally, to keep trust property separate, to invest with prudence, and to report and account. Section 16400 opens Chapter 4 of Part 4 of Division 9 of the Probate Code, titled "Liability of Trustees to Beneficiaries," which runs from section 16400 through section 16465 and is divided into articles on liability for breach of trust (§§ 16400-16403), remedies (§§ 16420-16421), the measure of liability (§§ 16440-16442), and limitations and exculpation (§§ 16460-16465). In Uzyel v. Kadisha, the Court of Appeal restated the section in the same terms while describing the duties a trustee owes. Whether any act or omission of Gregory T. Ahn violated a duty owed under the Lindeman Family Trust is a question this sheet does not answer.

WHEN A TRUSTEE ANSWERS FOR AN AGENT'S ACTS (PROB. CODE § 16401)
Probate Code section 16401, subdivision (a), states the general rule that the trustee is not liable to the beneficiary for the acts or omissions of an agent. Subdivision (b) then lists six circumstances in which the trustee is liable for an agent's act or omission that would be a breach of trust if the trustee had committed it: where the trustee directs the act; where the trustee delegates to the agent authority to perform an act the trustee is under a duty not to delegate; where the trustee does not use reasonable prudence in selecting or retaining the agent; where the trustee does not periodically review the agent's overall performance and compliance with the terms of the delegation; where the trustee conceals the act of the agent; and where the trustee, knowing of the agent's acts or omissions, neglects to take reasonable steps to compel the agent to redress the wrong. Subdivision (c) provides that liability for acts or omissions of agents occurring before July 1, 1987, is governed by prior law. Whether any person who performed work for the Lindeman Family Trust was an agent of Gregory T. Ahn within the meaning of this section, and whether any of the six circumstances existed, are questions this sheet does not answer.

WHEN A TRUSTEE ANSWERS FOR A COTRUSTEE'S BREACH (PROB. CODE § 16402)
Probate Code section 16402, subdivision (a), states that a trustee is not liable to the beneficiary for a breach of trust committed by a cotrustee, except in the circumstances subdivision (b) lists. Those five circumstances are participation in the cotrustee's breach; improper delegation of the administration of the trust to the cotrustee; approval of, knowing acquiescence in, or concealment of the cotrustee's breach; negligently enabling the cotrustee to commit a breach; and neglecting to take reasonable steps to compel the cotrustee to redress a breach where the trustee knows, or has information from which the trustee reasonably should have known, of it. Subdivision (c) leaves acts or omissions occurring before July 1, 1987, to prior law. Whether any cotrustee of the Lindeman Family Trust committed a breach, and whether any other trustee's conduct fell within one of those five circumstances, are questions this sheet does not answer.

WHEN A SUCCESSOR TRUSTEE ANSWERS FOR A PREDECESSOR'S BREACH (PROB. CODE § 16403)
Probate Code section 16403, subdivision (a), states that a successor trustee is not liable to the beneficiary for a breach of trust committed by a predecessor trustee, except in the three circumstances subdivision (b) lists: where the successor trustee knows, or has information from which the successor trustee reasonably should have known, of a situation constituting a predecessor's breach and improperly permits it to continue; where the successor trustee neglects to take reasonable steps to compel the predecessor to deliver the trust property to the successor; and where the successor trustee neglects to take reasonable steps to redress a predecessor's breach of which the successor knows or reasonably should have known. Subdivision (c) leaves acts or omissions occurring before July 1, 1987, to prior law. Whether Gregory T. Ahn succeeded a prior trustee of the Lindeman Family Trust, and whether any of those circumstances existed, are questions this sheet does not answer.

THE PROCEEDINGS A BENEFICIARY OR COTRUSTEE MAY BRING (PROB. CODE § 16420)
Probate Code section 16420, subdivision (a), provides that if a trustee commits a breach of trust, or threatens to commit one, a beneficiary or cotrustee of the trust may commence a proceeding for any of nine listed purposes that is appropriate: to compel the trustee to perform the trustee's duties; to enjoin the trustee from committing a breach; to compel the trustee to redress a breach by payment of money or otherwise; to appoint a receiver or temporary trustee to take possession of the trust property and administer the trust; to remove the trustee; subject to section 18100, to set aside acts of the trustee; to reduce or deny compensation of the trustee; subject to section 18100, to impose an equitable lien or a constructive trust on trust property; and, subject to section 18100, to trace trust property that has been wrongfully disposed of and recover the property or its proceeds. In Uzyel v. Kadisha, the Court of Appeal described the section as describing the basic remedies "in general terms" and said that the availability of a particular remedy and its application in particular circumstances are governed by the common law; the same opinion observed that disgorgement of a trustee's profits may be pursued through a money judgment under subdivision (a)(3) or through a judgment in rem under subdivision (a)(8) and (9). Which, if any, of those proceedings is available to a beneficiary of the Lindeman Family Trust is a question this sheet does not answer.

REMEDIES ARE IN EQUITY, AND THE STATUTORY LIST IS NOT EXCLUSIVE (PROB. CODE §§ 16420(B), 16421, 16442)
Two features of the statutory scheme sit alongside the list of proceedings in section 16420, subdivision (a). First, Probate Code section 16421 provides that the remedies of a beneficiary against the trustee are exclusively in equity. Second, the statutes twice say that the listed remedies do not displace others: section 16420, subdivision (b), provides that the provision of remedies for breach of trust in subdivision (a) does not prevent resort to any other appropriate remedy provided by statute or the common law, and section 16442 provides that the article stating the trustee's liability for breach of trust does not prevent resort to any other remedy available under the statutory or common law. The Court of Appeal in Uzyel v. Kadisha described section 16442 in those terms when it held that the absence of the words "with interest" from one measure of liability did not foreclose interest from another source. What either provision means for any claim concerning the Lindeman Family Trust is a question this sheet does not answer.

THE THREE MEASURES OF A TRUSTEE'S LIABILITY (PROB. CODE § 16440(A))
Probate Code section 16440, subdivision (a), provides that a trustee who commits a breach of trust is chargeable with any of three things that is appropriate under the circumstances: any loss or depreciation in value of the trust estate resulting from the breach, with interest; any profit made by the trustee through the breach, with interest; and any profit that would have accrued to the trust estate if the loss of profit is the result of the breach. In Uzyel v. Kadisha, the Court of Appeal read the phrase "is appropriate under the circumstances" as a grant of discretion to the trial court in selecting among the three measures, reviewable only for abuse of discretion. Which measure, if any, would be appropriate in a proceeding concerning the Lindeman Family Trust is a question this sheet does not answer.

DISGORGEMENT OF THE TRUSTEE'S OWN PROFIT, AND THE ABSENCE OF A TRACING REQUIREMENT (PROB. CODE § 16440(A)(2))
The second measure in Probate Code section 16440, subdivision (a), charges the trustee with any profit made by the trustee through the breach of trust, with interest. In Uzyel v. Kadisha the Court of Appeal construed the word "through": profits made through the misappropriation of trust funds are not limited to profits made by investing those particular funds or their proceeds, and the statutory language does not expressly impose a tracing requirement. The opinion's introduction states the same conclusion in one line. The court also rejected the argument that section 16420, subdivision (a)(9), which addresses tracing trust property that has been wrongfully disposed of, imports a tracing requirement into the measure of liability. Whether any profit was made through a breach in the administration of the Lindeman Family Trust is a question this sheet does not answer.

PROFIT THE TRUST WOULD HAVE MADE, AND APPRECIATION DAMAGES (PROB. CODE § 16440(A)(3))

It is prepared as background in connection with the Lindeman Family Trust dated June 14, 2011, the administration of that trust by Gregory T. Ahn, and any proceeding concerning it in Santa Clara County, California. It states what the statutes and the published opinions say. It does not state whether any particular act or omission was a breach of trust, what any trust instrument means, whether any claim is timely, or what any person should do.

Probate Code section 16400 states the whole of California's definition in one sentence: a violation by the trustee of any duty that the trustee owes the beneficiary is a breach of trust. The section does not list the duties; those are set out elsewhere in the Probate Code and in the trust instrument, and they include the duties to administer the trust according to its terms, to act loyally, to keep trust property separate, to invest with prudence, and to report and account. Section 16400 opens Chapter 4 of Part 4 of Division 9 of the Probate Code, titled "Liability of Trustees to Beneficiaries," which runs from section 16400 through section 16465 and is divided into articles on liability for breach of trust (§§ 16400-16403), remedies (§§ 16420-16421), the measure of liability (§§ 16440-16442), and limitations and exculpation (§§ 16460-16465). In Uzyel v. Kadisha, the Court of Appeal restated the section in the same terms while describing the duties a trustee owes. Whether any act or omission of Gregory T. Ahn violated a duty owed under the Lindeman Family Trust is a question this sheet does not answer.

expectedJSON.body: Three sections address the effect of a beneficiary's own conduct. Probate Code section 16463 provides that a beneficiary may not hold the trustee liable for an act or omission as a breach of trust if the beneficiary consented before or at the time of it, but lists three circumstances in which consent does not preclude liability — incapacity at the time of the consent or of the act, ignorance of the beneficiary's rights and of material facts that the trustee knew or should have known and did not reasonably believe the beneficiary knew, and consent induced by the trustee's improper conduct — and adds, where the trustee had an interest adverse to the beneficiary, that consent does not preclude liability where the transaction was not fair and reasonable to the beneficiary. Section 16464 applies a parallel structure to a release or contract discharging the trustee's liability, adding a fourth exception for a transaction involving a bargain with the trustee that was not fair and reasonable. Section 16465 does the same for a beneficiary who affirms a transaction the beneficiary could have rejected: the affirmance bars later rejection and liability for loss occurring after the trustee entered into the transaction, except in the same four circumstances. Whether any beneficiary of the Lindeman Family Trust consented to, released, or affirmed anything is a question this sheet does not answer.
